analysis.one_liner: Penalizes companies that move call center jobs overseas and makes agents tell callers where they are.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 25 cosponsors including one Republican, never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a public list of companies that move call center work overseas, cut those companies off from federal grants and guaranteed loans for five years, and give federal contracting preference to companies that keep call center jobs in the United States. It would also require federal contracts to keep call center work in the U.S., and require overseas customer-service agents to tell consumers where they are calling from and transfer them to a U.S.-based agent on request. The bill was sent to four House committees but never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. call center workers, who would see companies think twice before offshoring their jobs, and consumers, who would know whether the person on the phone is overseas and could ask to be transferred to a U.S. agent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. call center workers and consumers

how_it_helps.text: Companies that relocate or contract out call center work overseas would be named on a public Department of Labor list and barred from federal grants and guaranteed loans for five years [S2].
Federal agencies would have to prefer contractors that keep call center work in the U.S., and any call center work under a federal contract would have to be performed inside the United States [S2].

Agents outside the U.S. would have to disclose their physical location at the start of a customer service call, and consumers could request transfer to a U.S.-based agent, with the FTC enforcing violations as unfair or deceptive practices [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that offshore call center work, including the outsourcing industry that runs it, would face public listing, lost federal grants and loans, and new disclosure and compliance costs. Consumers could also see modestly higher service costs if companies onshore or automate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshoring companies and the outsourcing industry

drawbacks.text: Every business entity handling customer service calls would face new compliance duties — location disclosures, annual certifications to the FTC, and civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for failing to notify before offshoring — costs an honest supporter would acknowledge [S2].

Restricting call center work on federal contracts to the United States could raise costs for the government, and companies might respond to the penalties by automating customer service rather than keeping U.S. jobs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to U.S. workers and consumers are real but targeted: this would not ban offshoring, only make it costlier and more visible. The compliance burden on businesses is meaningful but conventional for consumer-disclosure rules, and the bill includes exceptions for all-U.S. operations, emergency services, and cases where a consumer knowingly calls a foreign agent [S2].

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee: it was referred to four House committees and then to an Energy and Commerce subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sharice Davids introduced the bill with Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick on May 8, 2024, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Oversight, and Armed Services Committees [S1].
On May 17, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S4].
The bill drew 25 cosponsors — 24 Democrats and 1 Republican — but never reached a committee vote or the House floor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that offshore call center jobs are better off: no public list, no five-year ban on federal grants and loans, no requirement that federal contract work stay in the U.S., and no mandatory location disclosures to callers. Federal contractors relying on overseas customer service also keep the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that offshore call center jobs

for.name: Rep. Sharice Davids
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan lead cosponsor.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its original Republican cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: House Oversight, Armed Services, and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote in the remainder of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor team was bipartisan — a Democrat and a Republican introduced it together — but 24 of the 25 cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Offshore call center and business process outsourcing firms
industries.note: Their business model depends on moving U.S. customer-service jobs abroad for cheaper labor. The bill would name companies on a public list, bar listed firms from federal grants and loans for five years, and require overseas agents to disclose their location to callers, directly cutting into that business.

industries.industry: U.S. companies that offshore customer service (retailers, telecoms, banks, tech firms)
industries.note: These companies lose access to federal grants and guaranteed loans for five years if they offshore call center work, and they bear new disclosure, certification, and penalty exposure. Some might onshore or automate, raising service costs. Their cost savings from offshore labor come at the expense of U.S. jobs and caller transparency, though the bill does not ban offshoring outright.

industries.industry: U.S.-based call center employees and domestic customer-service operations
industries.note: Federal contract call center work would have to be performed in the United States, and agencies would prefer contractors that do not offshore, supporting U.S. customer-service jobs. The bill also protects workers' existing federal benefits regardless of relocation.

industries.industry: Federal contractors relying on overseas call centers
industries.note: They would lose eligibility for contracts unless call center work is performed inside the U.S., raising their cost of delivering government services.
